turns.text: So it can extend further if the remedy at issue is the revocation of permission to be in the country. And I think the -- I think the reason for that is essentially this Court -- if you look at what is the -- the difference between public and private rights, I think, for the most part, the difference between public and private rights is that public rights involve the grant or denial of a benefit, which would include permission to be in the country. Private rights involve things that impose -- that deal with life, liberty, and property. At the margins, the Court has recognized that there are areas where public rights can involve taking money, like tax liability, tariffs, things like that that I think complicate the line, but what the Court has said is that in those areas at the margins, that's where we look to history. And so --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Can I -- can I ask you this? Suppose I disagree with you that there is an analogy here to a contract. What -- can you win the case?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yes. And --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Explain how that is.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I think we can still win the case on that ground because it's still penalties. And so the Court, in -- in Tull, as Justice Kavanaugh was suggesting, said that penalties were always a traditional remedy at common law. And I think back wages also are a traditional common law -- or even if not -- I think there's a dispute between the parties, are they legal or equitable? You know, we think they are legal. But, even if they're --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: So just to make sure I understand, Mr. Johnson, you're saying that as a backup to your contract argument, assuming your contract argument is off the table, is rejected, you're saying your backup argument is just these involve penalties; therefore, there cannot be administrative adjudication. Is that correct?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: That's correct. Again, I don't --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: But that's not what Jarkesy said. Jarkesy, you know, could have said that, but it didn't say that. It said: We understand that there are various kinds of historic exceptions. One of them is immigration; another might be Customs; another might be taxation. The one we're talking about here is immigration. But Jarkesy was very clear. It could have gone further. It did not go further. It said that there are these historic places where there's a different kind of analysis.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yeah, and so I don't dispute that there are historical areas where liability can be imposed outside the Article III courts, but I think that with those areas that there has to be a careful attention to history and to what was going on in those -- in those cases. And I think, if you look at Oceanic Steam, you know, Justice Barrett mentioned the -- the quote from Oceanic Steam that I think, you know, I had picked out as well, to my mind, as the most important line in that opinion. The other line that I think is critical in that opinion is the final line of the opinion, which says that the Court is not deciding questions that would decide if -- that would arise, excuse me, if the government were to endow administrative officers with the power to enforce a lawful exaction by methods which were not within the competency of administrative duties because they require the exercise of judicial power. And I think that is exactly the distinction that the Court was drawing there, that the -- that the -- the factual determination that was made in that case was a factual determination about whether to allow the aliens into the border or not, which was within the core of the executive's immigration power, and then the collection of the -- of the penalty was a exaction upon permission to recross the border, so also involved an exercise of the --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Mr. Johnson --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I mean, I don't --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Oh, please.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: No, please.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So is it your position that in the historic exception buckets that Justice Kagan identified, you simply can't have civil penalties? Like, so, for example, here, you agree it's not really that you're drawing a line at the border for immigration because you agree that someone could be removed from the country in an executive proceeding, right?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: That's correct.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Okay. So it's really about what the government is seeking to do here, and that's the imposition of a civil penalty. So your position is that in the immigration context, even though that is a public rights exception for some purposes, civil penalties are not okay within that context, is that right?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: That is, although, again, I don't think the Court needs to go that far because --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Is that true in every one of the historical -- I mean, how broad is your argument? Is that true for all of the public rights exceptions?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: I'm not making an argument about other exceptions that aren't at issue here because my reading of Jarkesy is that each of those exceptions has to be taken on its own terms. So, for instance, the tax exception, you know, rests on a very different ground where taxes could be collected by the -- the tax inspector in the first instance. So I think you might have an instance where, you know, a tax penalty would be viewed differently. I don't know. I think what -- the way I read Jarkesy is there are no kind of overarch -- the overarching principle here is Article III and that the exceptions are exceptions that have to be --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But, if it's okay in some of these categories -- and this was -- you know, I asked Ms. Harris whether there was a mix and match -- whether it was okay to mix and match a little bit. Say, like, well, this is an immigration bucket, but it also bears a resemblance to public benefits, and so we can look that this kind of thing would be okay there, so it's okay here too. Why, once we're in a public rights exception like immigration, can't we say, like, okay, it's all on the table for administrative adjudication?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Because I think that's the kinds of reasoning that, you know, if you take -- well, this was okay over here in the tax context and this was over -- okay over here in the tariff context and then you kind of put them all together, that's how I think the courts arrived --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So it's isolated? They're islands? You have to look at each one and decide, and which bucket would you put this in? Would you put this in government benefits or would you put this in immigration?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I would put this in neither. But I think that the relevant -- I don't think there is a public benefits -- well, there's a public benefits exception in the sense of, you know, awarding --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: -- benefits or not. But I don't know that there's sort of like a government privileges exception, like the -- the government suggests there is. I don't know that that exception even exists. So I think the exception that we would be construing here would be the immigration exception.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: And you're -- so you're not arguing, just so I'm clear, that, as Justice Kagan points out, Jarkesy didn't go this far. You're not arguing that in this case we should say all civil penalties must be in Article III?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: No. I don't think that it --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Okay. So you recognize the exceptions. And immigration -- assume immigration's the relevant exception. And then you're saying we have to -- what's the rule for civil penalties in the immigration context?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I think the Court should look --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Because I think you said, well, in that context, all civil penalties must be Article III. Did you say that?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So -- and here I think is where I would --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Is that just -- can I just get an answer to that?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yeah. Could I just distinguish between the rule that I would advocate and then how I think --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Can you say yes or no to him? Because I thought I heard you say that too.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Yeah, that was --

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Can you just answer that yes or no? In the immigration context, are you arguing that all civil penalties must be Article III?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yes, but I don't think the Court should go that far in this case. So what I'm saying is that my view --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Now you can explain that.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Okay. So my view is that the Court indicated that the exceptions have to be applied with careful attention to history, so I think I look at -- you know, if you look at the history here, so I take the Alien Friends Act, which I think is the key precedent for understanding the scope of the -- the immigration adjudication doctrine, and the Alien Friends Act from 1798 drew a very clear distinction where the President could deport, but Section 4 said that -- that offenses against the Act would be prosecuted in the Article III courts, and Section 5 said that nothing the President did when deporting an alien would have any impact on the alien's property rights in the United States. And so I think the Alien Friends Act, 1798, draws a fairly clear distinction between the executive's power to deport and then actions that affect property.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: One -- one problem or concern, I guess, is a better way to say it about what you just said -- and Ms. Harris alluded to this -- is, if we're looking for clarity, what you're proposing there is really at war with clarity. There's going to be a lot of guesswork about where exactly within, let's say, the immigration exception or within the other exceptions the line's drawn. And I think that's not great systemically going forward. So can you answer that concern?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I see, really, two key distinctions. I take Oceanic Steam to be the high-water mark of the immigration adjudication doctrine when it comes to penalties. And I see two key distinctions between this case and Oceanic. This Court could emphasize both in its opinion, or it could emphasize either with different implications for other penalties, other immigration penalties. So the Court could emphasize the fact that the -- the nature of the claims was focused on crossing the border or not crossing the border, or it could emphasize that the nature of the remedy was an exaction at the border, or it could emphasize both. I think the best reading is to emphasize both because I think that both were salient features of -- of Oceanic. However, I think, if the Court were, for instance, to emphasize the nature of the claims, then that would have different downstream effects than if the Court was to emphasize the nature of the remedies.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: What you're outlining is kind of a hodgepodge opinion, and, you know, maybe sometimes courts write that sort of thing. But, to follow the --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Not ever us.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: -- to follow the train of this -- of your recent colloquy, so you say that it is not true or at least it is not necessary for us to true that civil penalties always require adjudication in an Article III court. And then you say: And, in fact, it's not true or it's not necessary for us to say that this is always necessary in the immigration context. But, in the immigration context, there's a limit beyond which -- that cannot be exceeded, and that is set by the Alien Friends Act. So it has to be just like the Alien Friends Act? No.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: No.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: By his- -- by the relevant history?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yeah. So I guess what I'm saying is that I -- I think that the -- if you chart the history from the Alien Friends Act up to Oceanic, I take Oceanic to be the high-water mark.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: And why is it the high-water mark? I know you don't want us to go any further, but why is it the high-water mark? What -- what is it about the rationale of Oceanic Steam that makes it the high-water mark?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Well, so I take the test to be history. And I think, you know, Oceanic, to my mind, is already pretty late in the historical game, but it's -- this Court in Jarkesy identified it as relevant history in this context. So I -- I think the tradition in Oceanic, you know, is something the Court has accepted. But I don't -- I don't think the doctrine of immigration adjudication -- if there are salient differences between what was going on there in terms of the claims and the remedies. But, like I said, I think the Court could write an opinion that is -- that is much more narrow than that and that --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: The problem is I don't know what the relevant history is for you. Oceanic was at a time when immigration was totally different. If you finally put your foot on U.S. soil, you were here. And deportation was a very different process, if at all, I mean, because we didn't have all the problems we've had. But almost as soon as immigration began to be a problem -- in this case, the -- these regulations have been around since 1988 -- 1986, I think. It's a long time. There have been administrative processes that have imposed fines for employers who have lied about bringing people in.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So, you know, actually, I don't think that's the history that -- that -- you know, the -- the first immigration-related penalties that we're aware of that are -- you know, that -- where there were prohibitions on bringing certain types of people into the country is the Foran Act in 1875, and it provided for judicial -- judicial --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Yes, because that's what was going on.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Can I just ask you another species of a question? Because I -- I guess I'm not sure how you are employing history. What is the work of it? Mr. Chief Justice?

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Briefly.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: In the context of your analysis. On the one hand, from your opening, it suggested -- and maybe even here it suggested that you're looking for a -- an historical analog to what is actually going on here, and the government can't enforce in ways that we don't find historically. That's one way. But then there's another way, I guess, which is we're looking at history for the criteria that one should apply when determining whether or not this is a public or private benefit. So which -- which are you doing?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I think you have to look at each exception on its own terms, and then I think you're looking at the exception to see essentially what is the -- the rationale. And I do think you -- it can't just be --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So it's the rationale. It's not that you're saying that Oceanic Steam -- that we have to have a -- an enforcement scheme that looks exactly like Oceanic Steam in order to fit into this exception?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: I'm not saying that Oceanic Steam involves steamships. What I'm saying is that it involved -- both the claim and the remedy involved the exercise of the executive's power to control who could come over the border or not.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Your friend, Ms. Harris, put a lot of chips on the table when she finished saying this would be quite destructive for the government if she lost. One, I want to make sure you've said everything you can, with response particularly to Justice Kavanaugh, about why, from your perspective, you don't think that would be such a big deal but then also to get your thoughts on how destructive it would be for the individual rights involved if you did not prevail.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Okay. So, you know, in terms of the impact of this, maybe, first, I could focus on immigration. So I think there are -- you know, for the most part, immigration adjudication involves the question of whether to admit, exclude, or deport, and that includes deportate -- deporting something based on things that happened after they enter the country. I don't think any of that is problematic because none of it involves -- it all involves classic public -- public rights, whether to allow someone into or out of the country. When it comes to immigration penalties, I think that the effect -- the sweep of the Court's decision depends on whether the Court focuses on the nature of the -- you know, as I suggest, the nature of the claims and the remedies in Oceanic or if you just focus on the nature of the claims. If the Court were to just focus on the nature of the claims, then I think that would leave, for instance -- the 1324(a), (b), and (c) penalties for employing unlawful immigrants would be undisturbed, for instance, because the nature of the claim there turns on the -- the employment -- the -- whether the person is in the country lawfully or not. So I think those don't necessarily rise or fall with what the Court would do in this case. I think, similarly, like, penalties for a false statement in -- in an immigration application could be meaningfully distinct. So I don't think all of that has to rise and fall with this case. I think, you know, beyond that, the government -- a lot of the penalties the government points to are reasonably distinct for a lot of different reasons. Many of them are withholding money. So the government may -- has a contract with somebody and they withhold money that they owe under the contract as a penalty. I think that's just a completely distinct sort of situation. You know, the government talks about tax. I think tax is just a completely distinct area of the law that rests on a different historical foundation. So I -- I think that -- I don't think that the decision here is going to decide all of that. In terms of the -- the impact of the government's theory, I think especially when it comes to the sort of government's broader theory that anytime there's a condition or a benefit we can just attach privileges -- or, excuse me, conditions to that and then leverage the -- the fact of the condition to require non-Article III adjudication, that's going to just have all kinds of consequences. I think the fact that the government in their brief says that access to the mail, I think, really puts a point on -- that access to the mail is a privilege really puts a point on it. If you think of all the criminal laws that penalize using the mail to do various things and how broad that criminal jurisdiction sweeps, the government seems to be suggesting they could do the same thing with penalties outside of Article III, that if you send something through the mail, there's all these conditions on it, and then we can -- we can penalize that through outside the Article III courts.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Putting aside penalties, if the government simply decertified you, would you have the same arguments?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: No.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: If you signed a contract saying the government could impose penalties, would you have the same argument?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I think that's a great question, and I think that it would turn on the unconstitutional conditions doctrine.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Mm-hmm.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: And I think it would be -- you know, there -- it would --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So you -- you're an employer who wants to treat these workers as badly as he or she can, so just sign the contract because you'll have to rely on the Justice Department having enough lawyers to get to everybody who does that?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Well, so I just think the -- you know, whether the -- the government could require this as a -- as a condition --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right. Can I ask one final question?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: The -- you seem to be suggesting that we have to write this to let some of the penalties in the statute survive but not this one? Is that correct? You said there are some of the penalties in the statute that would be okay under your theory, but others would not.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: I was referring to the -- they're not at issue in this case. I was referring to the -- there's a series of penalties that are adjudicated administratively under 8 U.S.C. 1324(a), (b), (c) that I think are --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Okay. So Justice Kavanaugh was right, we're going to have to write very carefully to win -- to let you win.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan?

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I have to tell you, Mr. Johnson, I'm still struggling with the argument a little bit. You said the difference between this case and Oceanic is the nature of the claims and the nature of the remedies. The nature of the claims, you said, well, Oceanic was an admissions case. Of course, the government has complete authority to use administrative adjudications with respect to admissions. Well, this is an admissions case. An employer has gone to the government and said: We're going to make various certifications so that you allow us to bring in a boatload of foreign workers. Those -- and -- and -- and what the government is now saying is those admissions requirements that we put on the admission of these workers has been violated. And just the same way that the admissions requirement in Oceanic has been violated, so too here, and so the same penalties can apply. You said it's the remedies question. The remedy there was civil fines. The remedy here is civil fines. So, you know, we -- we -- we -- we have the -- the -- the factual difference that this is occurring not at the border itself, but this is essentially the government saying you have violated admissions pledges that you've made to us, without which we would not have allowed these people in because we would think that these people would undercut the economic status of domestic workers. You violated that admissions criterion, so you pay the price.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So, you know, I -- I think that that's wrong for a few reasons. And maybe one way to see, I think, that illustrates that it's wrong is that not all these workers are even immigrant workers, that over a third of them are domestic workers. You know, another way I think that illustrates that that's not the right way to think about it is that if you -- you know, here, if you have the inspection that finds these violations, it doesn't result in deporting the workers. You know, the workers can -- can stay. They can continue to work. It's just that the -- the -- they found a violation of the working conditions. It's not -- you know, it's not like --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Because we think that once you pay the penalty, you -- you know, you will no longer violate the admissions criteria.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Well, whether that's true or not, my point is that this is not a -- it's not a deportable offense. And even if the government was to say, oh, this is so bad that we're going to terminate the contract, the H-2A laws allow a worker to -- to transfer from one employer to another employer, so these workers could still stay in the country working for a different employer.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I mean, I feel that at the base of your argument, Mr. Johnson, you're trying to get us to think that the H-2A program is not an immigration program. But it is an immigration program. It's all about when do we allow the admission of foreign workers given the fact that we're concerned that foreign workers will undercut the economic status of domestic workers. That's the program. It's about the admission of foreign workers.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So, you know, I don't disagree that immigration is part of what's going on here, but I think, under that theory or under that sort of description, that the claims at issue in Stern would have been bankruptcy claims. You know, I -- I don't think that it's a sort of subject matter test. I think that you need to look closely at what's the nature of the claim, what's the nature of the remedy, what's actually going on in this case, and what's going on in this case is not about the executive's exercise of the power over the immigration into the country.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Gorsuch?

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Let me see if I got it. The government wants to expel or prevent admission of somebody, no problem?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: If they want to put in a penalty because you violated a term of entry or whatnot, like in Oceanic, as an alternative for that, that's fine too?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So, again, this is where it goes to whether, I think, you focus on the -- the nature of the claim or the collection remedy.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah, I understand.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: But -- but it could be okay?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yes. Yes.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. And the problem here is we're adjudicating a contract or something that looks an awful lot like a contract between an employer and an employee?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: And some of those employees are American citizens?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: And it doesn't wind up -- however -- whatever happens as a result of this adjudication, nobody will be admitted or deported?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: In terms of the difference between you and the government on how this would operate, I just want to make sure I have this clear. You agree that even under the government's approach, you can get judicial review. The differences are who initiates, I suppose, the court proceedings and then whether the standard of review will be de novo or deferential once you get to court, correct?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yes. So I think, under this Court's decision in FCC, there's no question that an agency can have proceedings to decide whether to initiate enforcement action in court, and I -- I don't think we contest that. The problem here is that you don't -- don't -- you don't then get a de novo proceeding in court.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Right. So you get judicial review. The question about standard of review is really what is going to be the -- the key difference in practical operation depending on which side wins here, correct?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Okay. And then I just want to make sure I have this straight. You said that we can rule for you and at the same time hold or suggest or indicate that penalties on employers for -- under 1324 for employing people unlawfully in the country or not verifying their status could still be done by administrative adjudication without an Article III court, correct?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Yeah. So, again, it's -- in my view, that is not the correct way to decide the case, but I think it is an available way to decide the case. And then --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: And then the principle if we did say that would be?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Would be that -- that you look at the nature of the claim and ask whether the nature of the claim is about immigration status, whether someone is lawfully in the country or not or can lawfully be -- be in the country. And so that was the nature of the claim in Oceanic. I think in a case about -- you know, if the allegation is that the -- the worker was unlawfully employed, fundamentally, the allegation is this worker was not lawfully in the country.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Based on your answers just now to Justice Kavanaugh and earlier to Justice Gorsuch, now I'm starting to think there's really not that much difference between the Solicitor General or the government's position about germaneness and your argument because what I kind of hear you saying along the way as you're distinguishing with Justice Kagan and you're talking to Justice Kavanaugh is, well, this just seems pretty far removed from the heartland of telling someone they either can't get in or they have to be removed from the country. So is there much of a difference in your position now between this germaneness line the government would draw?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So, to be clear, I think my position of what the best reading here is that I would focus both on the nature of the claim and the remedy because I -- I do think, when you're only looking at the claim, that is -- there is a certain risk that it gets a little bit indeterminate. So, you know, I think, if you look at the nature of the remedy, that that's -- that really -- the fact that Oceanic was --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So, wait, like, let me just clarify to make sure I understand what you're saying. You're saying, if you looked at the remedy, like your first-line position would be, listen, civil penalties, even in the context of immigration, are just always out. They always have to go to Article III. If you lose that, however, your position seems awfully like the government's germaneness test.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I do think it's different. I think that my view would be the question is, is it -- is the claim about whether somebody is lawfully in the country or not, or is it otherwise about sort of the process of determining whether someone is lawfully in the country or not? I think that's different from germaneness, which I take to be kind of more of like what is the degree of separation, which, you know, I -- I don't think is an administrable standard because I don't know, you know, is that a rational basis test? Is it some sort of more tight test? I don't know what germaneness really means.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Okay. Thanks.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So are foreign workers who are brought into the country pursuant to a set of conditions that are subsequently violated lawfully in the country?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So they would be, yes. So an H-2A --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: They would be?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So an H-2A worker, if they come into the country under --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Pursuant to a set of conditions that allows for their entry that are subsequently violated --

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- they are lawfully in the country?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: Well, so, you know, I guess maybe I'm not understanding the question right. If your question is --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: No, I think you understand the question. I think it just really highlights why "lawfully in the country" can't be the right line for --

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- determining whether or not this is an immigration case.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: -- if an H-2A worker is working at a farm that has violated these terms and conditions, the H-2A worker is not in the country unlawfully. The H-2A worker could, you know, if the -- if the government is -- the government has a choice, to -- to debar someone from the program --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I thought the government could expel them. They -- if you agree that the government could expel them, it would be because the conditions are violated and, therefore, they are not in the country lawfully, right?

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So, under the statute, to expel someone for these types of violations, the government has to prove that they're substantial.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Okay.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: And so, if the government can't prove that the violations are substantial, the -- the employment contract would not end.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Let me ask you another question. I hear you setting up a test for identifying public rights that turns on the nature or the claim -- of the claim or the remedies. You've said it many times. That's like how we should tell courts to go about doing this. What I don't understand is where those particular criteria come from because, in the historical cases, those were not the metric. You just seem to be looking at the historical cases and picking out certain facts and telling us that today we should have a new test that relates to those facts. But we have many, many cases in which public route -- rights were applied and found by this Court even though the government imposed monetary liability. So it was not tied to the remedy as to whether or not you would find a public right. We have many cases that resembled common-law claims, and the Court still found that there were public rights involved. So help me to understand whether you are asking us to just fashion a new test based on some facts that you see in the historical cases. Surely, this is not what we were doing traditionally because those cases would have come out differently.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I think that there are -- that most of the cases that you're referencing arise in a distinct historical tradition bucket, you might say.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Right. But they don't turn on the factors that you're now saying we should apply. That's my -- I'm trying to help the courts that Justice Kavanaugh says are going to be confused. So I want to have a rule, like, what do you look for to determine whether or not this is a public rights case or a private rights case? And you have offered us one. You say: Look at the nature of the claim and the type of remedy. And I say: Ha, that rule's not going to work consistent with all the public right -- rights cases that we have traditionally had because those cases wouldn't be public rights if your test is -- is -- is the right test. So I guess I'm just trying to understand what you're asking us to do and isn't it novel.

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: So I don't think it's novel. I think, if you actually look at those historical cases, they do turn on distinct considerations. So, for instance, just to pick one, the government cites McElrath, which is a case about the dispute between the government and a government employee and whether the Court of Claims could adjudicate counterclaims, and it's about -- the case is about the importance of the government's sovereign immunity, that, you know, there's particular considerations --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Right, but you're --

turns.name: ROBERT E. JOHNSON
turns.text: -- involving government employees --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- not asking us to look at those considerations. I'm just trying to figure out where you're getting your test from, but I think I have the answer. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, Ms. Harris?

turns.name: SARAH M. HARRIS
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. Three points. One is a 40,000-foot point. It would be a big deal for the government to lose, but an even bigger deal would be to have a mess, to have no clarity as to what the scope of public rights looks like, no sense of what's left of Atlas Roofing, how it fits in on things, no sense of what -- what part of history, what the historical test looks like to even define otherwise accepted categories of public rights. The government cannot live like that. We have too many schemes involving civil penalties, involving things that historically have analogized to public rights, to live under uncertainty because we have an accumulating number of cases that could be subject years from now to complete wipeout if we don't have additional certainty. So it is quite important to us. Please give additional certainty on the high-level score along the lines Justice Jackson was just talking about. Second, how should you rule in this case? I think there's a pretty clear contrast at this point. We have -- we have attempted to articulate a fairly clear rule. You look at the historical categories of public rights. There are two that everyone agrees are implicated here. One is immigration. Everyone agrees that it includes admission and exclusion of aliens. I don't think there is any way to conceive of that right that would not also include the fact that once someone is admitted, they can also be removed or be ineligible to remain based on conditions that the government prescribes. That's a very clear, a very well-established body of cases. It's the zenith of Article I and II powers together. The second line is public privileges and benefits. I think the two working together makes this an easier case rather than a harder one. When you are piggybacking on a -- on a quintessential public right, when you are using the government's power over immigration to allow someone not just into the country but to remain on a visa only so long as they are doing the work at your farm during the growing season, that you have promised to comply with various conditions, the Court has accepted the -- that you have to take the bitter with the sweet. Once you get that privilege, you've agreed to adjudicate violations of that, and you are subject to the conditions in executive adjudication. That's Oceanic Steam but a whole body of cases that Oceanic Steam is built from that establish that. I think that's all you need to say to resolve the case. The other side of this is a true hodgepodge. I'm not quite sure what the lines would look like. I think Respondent has now given up on no civil penalties at all in executive adjudications. That would be overturning all sorts of precedents where they've been allowed. I -- I'm not sure where Respondent has landed on when civil penalties are fine. If they're fine in the immigration context, if so, when? If there's a test for looking exactly like Oceanic Steam, if there's certain criteria in Oceanic Steam beyond not looking like a steamship that would be material, I'm not sure why that would be. That's certainly not the way the Court has ever interpreted Oceanic Steam ever since then. But that gets us to the situation of a mess. If the government, every time it wants to adjudicate civil penalties or invoke things that are historically part of the public rights doctrine, has to look through cases and try to guess which factual distinction is going to be -- become the basis for this is a bridge too far, we have no predictability for what we're supposed to do. We need to be able to structure our operations on this stuff because it affects so many cases, so many resources, the power of the executive branch, and our relationship with the courts and how courts' resources are impacted. So, please, clear lines. That's what I'm asking for here. Finally, a word on remedies. I don't like the prospect of losing. I think that's very obvious. I hope we don't lose this case because of the consequences. But, if you were looking to, you know, which poison is the least bad, I agree that the poison that's the least bad is at least saying that we can impose penalties initially in adjudications and then have de novo review in Article III courts. I will just tell you, though, that could work in certain contexts, but it's not a real fix across the board. There are very hard questions for a lot of other statutory regimes that could also be on the cutting-room floor for executive adjudication, where we would have to go to Congress. And that -- that's a -- you know, please tell us now if we -- if we need to get Legislative Affairs on it right now because this will snowball. Please reverse.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.
